enc.title: Read 7.1–7.2: unitary representations; SO(3) and its Lie algebra

blocks.html:
• Why must a symmetry act by unitary operators that compose like the group?
  • How do you get from a rotation group to commutators like $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$?

Script (German) 7.1–7.2, pp. 66–69. Look for: $U(g_1)U(g_2)=U(g_1g_2)$, rotations $R(\vec e,\omega)=e^{\omega\Omega(\vec e)}$, the generators $\Omega_j$ and their commutators (the Lie algebra so(3)), and how $U(R)=e^{-i\omega\vec e\cdot\vec L/\hbar}$ turns them into angular momentum. If the lecturer’s chapter 7 pack is installed, the strip at the top links the explainers for this section.

Why are the generators of rotations in $\mathcal H$ hermitian?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$U(R(\vec e,\omega))=e^{-i\omega\vec e\cdot\vec M}$ is unitary for all $\omega$; differentiating $U^\dagger U=\mathbb 1$ at $\omega=0$ gives $M^\dagger=M$.</details>

Which property of rotations makes the Lie algebra non-abelian?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Rotations about different axes do not commute; to second order the commutator of two infinitesimal rotations is a rotation about the third axis: $[\Omega_1,\Omega_2]=\Omega_3$, which becomes $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar L_3$.</details>

• What does “irreducible” mean, and why does unitarity let you split a representation?
  • Why must $j$ be a half-integer or integer?

Script (German) 7.3–7.4, pp. 70–74. Look for: invariant subspaces and their complements, ladder operators $M_\pm$, the top state $M_+\psi_j=0$, the Casimir $\vec M^2=j(j+1)$, $\dim\mathcal D_j=2j+1$. If the lecturer’s chapter 7 pack is installed, the strip at the top links the explainers for this section.

Derive $\vec M^2=j(j+1)$ on the top state.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\vec M^2=M_-M_++M_3^2+M_3$; on $\psi_j$ with $M_+\psi_j=0$, $M_3\psi_j=j\psi_j$: $\vec M^2\psi_j=(j^2+j)\psi_j$. It commutes with all $M_k$, so it is $j(j+1)$ on the whole irreducible space.</details>

Why does the ladder down from $m=j$ have to stop exactly at $m=-j$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\|M_-\psi_m\|^2=j(j+1)-m(m-1)$ must not be negative; the chain must end with $M_-\psi_{m_0}=0$, i.e. $m_0=-j$. From $j$ to $-j$ in integer steps: $2j$ is an integer.</details>

enc.title: Read 7.5–7.7: SO(3) vs SU(2), projective representations, spin

blocks.html:
• How can a rotation by $2\pi$ act as $-\mathbb 1$ without contradicting anything measurable?
  • What is the double cover, concretely?

Script (German) 7.5–7.7, pp. 75–79. Look for: $\tilde x=x^j\sigma_j$ and $\tilde x\mapsto A\tilde xA^\dagger$, the kernel $\{\pm\mathbb 1\}$, $e^{-2\pi iM_3}=(-1)^{2j}$, the cocycle condition, the spin of the electron on $L^2(\mathbb R^3)\otimes\mathbb C^2$. If the lecturer’s chapter 7 pack is installed, the strip at the top links the explainers for this section.

Compute $e^{-i\pi\sigma_3}$ and interpret it.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\mathrm{diag}(e^{-i\pi},e^{i\pi})=-\mathbb 1$: the rotation by $2\pi$ on spin $\frac12$. The overall sign does not change any probability, so it is allowed: $\mathcal D_{1/2}$ is a projective representation of SO(3), an honest one of SU(2).</details>

Why do the spherical harmonics only have integer $l$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$Y_{lm}\propto e^{im\varphi}$ must be single-valued on the sphere, so $m$ and $l$ are integers. Spin is not a function on the sphere.</details>

options: projective representations of SO(3) (honest ones of SU(2))

blocks.html:
• What is the weakest thing a symmetry must preserve?
  • Why are rotations represented unitarily and never anti-unitarily?

Script (German) 7.8, pp. 80–81. Look for: transition probabilities on rays, unitary or anti-unitary, the square argument (Weyl’s lemma), time reversal as the anti-unitary example. If the lecturer’s chapter 7 pack is installed, the strip at the top links the explainers for this section.

Why does an anti-unitary operator still preserve probabilities?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\langle U\phi|U\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle\phi|\psi\rangle}$ has the same modulus.</details>

Give the argument that every rotation is unitary.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$U(g)^2$ is unitary even if $U(g)$ is anti-unitary, so $U(g^2)\propto U(g)^2$ is unitary; every rotation is the square of the rotation by half the angle.</details>

enc.title: Read 8.1–8.2: relative coordinates and the Coulomb potential

blocks.html:
• Why does a two-body problem become a one-body problem?
  • What do the limits $r\to0$ and $r\to\infty$ tell you before solving anything?

Script (German) 8.1–8.2, pp. 82–87. Look for: centre of mass and reduced mass, separation $\Psi=\frac{u(r)}rY_{lm}$, the effective potential with $\frac{\hbar^2l(l+1)}{2mr^2}$, the behaviour at $r=0$ (8.2.1) and $r\to\infty$ (8.2.2), the terminating series and $E_n=-\frac{me^4}{2\hbar^2n^2}$.

Why $u\sim r^{l+1}$ at small $r$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>The centrifugal term dominates: $u^{\prime\prime}\approx\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u$, so $u=r^{l+1}$ or $r^{-l}$; the second is not allowed (not normalisable for $l\ge1$, and for $l=0$ it would need a $\delta$ source).</details>

Where does the degeneracy $n^2$ come from?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$E$ depends only on $n=n_r+l+1$; for given $n$, $l=0,\dots,n-1$ with $2l+1$ values of $m$: $\sum(2l+1)=n^2$. The $l$-degeneracy is the hidden symmetry of 8.3.</details>

How does the radial asymptotics differ from the 3D oscillator (sheet 10)?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Hydrogen: $u\sim e^{-\kappa r}$ (exponential), bound states only for $E<0$ and a continuum above. Oscillator: Gaussian $e^{-m\omega r^2/2\hbar}$ and a purely discrete spectrum.</details>

check.q: Bohr radius in the script’s units

blocks.html:
• Rotations explain the $m$-degeneracy. What explains that different $l$ have the same energy?
  • What is conserved besides $\vec L$?

Script (German) 8.3, pp. 88–92. Look for: the Pauli-Lenz vector $\vec J$, its algebra on a fixed energy $E<0$, $\vec S=\frac12(\vec L+a\vec J)$, $\vec D=\frac12(\vec L-a\vec J)$ with $a=\sqrt{-m/2E}$, $\vec S^2=\vec D^2$ and the energies from the Casimir.

Why does $\vec S^2=\vec D^2$, and what does it give for the multiplets?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\vec S^2-\vec D^2=a\vec L\cdot\vec J=0$ since $\vec J\perp\vec L$. So both su(2) have the same spin $s$: the eigenspace is $\mathcal D_s\otimes\mathcal D_s$ of dimension $(2s+1)^2=n^2$ with $n=2s+1$.</details>
Which $l$ appear in $\mathcal D_s\otimes\mathcal D_s$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\vec L=\vec S+\vec D$: $l=0,1,\dots,2s=n-1$, exactly the hydrogen multiplet.</details>

blocks.html:
• How does a rotation act on a two-particle state?
  • Why do two spins $\frac12$ give spin 1 and spin 0?

Script (German) 9.1–9.3, pp. 93–97. Look for: $\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2$, total generators $\vec J=\vec J^{(1)}\otimes\mathbb 1+\mathbb 1\otimes\vec J^{(2)}$, the highest-weight method, triplet and singlet.

Build the triplet and the singlet with $S_-=S_-^{(1)}+S_-^{(2)}$.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$|1,1\rangle=|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle$, $S_-$ gives $|1,0\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle+|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$, $|1,-1\rangle=|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$. The orthogonal $m=0$ state $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$ is killed by $S_+$: the singlet.</details>

Eigenvalues of $\vec S_1\cdot\vec S_2$ on triplet and singlet?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\frac12(S^2-S_1^2-S_2^2)$: $\frac{\hbar^2}2(2-\frac32)=\frac{\hbar^2}4$ and $\frac{\hbar^2}2(0-\frac32)=-\frac34\hbar^2$.</details>

• Which total $j$ appear in $\mathcal D_{j_1}\otimes\mathcal D_{j_2}$, and how do you check it?
  • How are Clebsch-Gordan coefficients computed without tables?

Script (German) 9.4–9.5, pp. 98–101. Look for: the series $|j_1-j_2|\le j\le j_1+j_2$, counting by $m$ multiplicities and dimensions, the coefficients $\langle j_1m_1;j_2m_2|j,m\rangle$ and the simple example 9.5.1.

Check $\mathcal D_1\otimes\mathcal D_1=\mathcal D_2\oplus\mathcal D_1\oplus\mathcal D_0$ by counting.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Dimensions $9=5+3+1$; $m$ multiplicities for $m=2,1,0$: $1,2,3$, so one top state each for $j=2,1,0$.</details>

Find $|\frac32,\frac12\rangle$ in $1\otimes\frac12$.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Apply $J_-$ to $|1\rangle|\uparrow\rangle$: $J_-|\frac32,\frac32\rangle=\sqrt3|\frac32,\frac12\rangle=\sqrt2|0\rangle|\uparrow\rangle+|1\rangle|\downarrow\rangle$, so $|\frac32,\frac12\rangle=\sqrt{\frac23}|0\rangle\uparrow+\sqrt{\frac13}|1\rangle\downarrow$.</details>

enc.title: Read 9.6–9.7: magnetic moment, Zeeman effect, spin-orbit coupling

blocks.html:
• Where does a magnetic moment come from in the Hamiltonian?
  • Why does the anomalous Zeeman effect need $g\approx2$ and $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$?

Script (German) 9.6–9.7, pp. 102–107. Look for: minimal coupling (9.39), $\vec M=\frac q{2mc}\vec L$ (9.46), $H_Z=-\vec M\cdot\vec B$ (9.47), $\Delta E_Z=\mu_BB_zm$ (9.50), spin moment with $g$ (9.52), spin-orbit coupling and $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(\vec J^2-\vec L^2-\vec S^2)$.

Why is $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ diagonal in the $|j,m_j\rangle$ basis but not in $|m_l,m_s\rangle$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(\vec J^2-\vec L^2-\vec S^2)$ commutes with $\vec J^2$ and $J_z$, but not with $L_z$ or $S_z$ separately. Eigenvalue $\frac{\hbar^2}2[j(j+1)-l(l+1)-\frac34]$.</details>

Weak field vs strong field (Paschen-Back): which basis?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Weak $B$: spin-orbit dominates, $|j,m_j\rangle$ with $\Delta E=g_{lj}\mu_BBm_j$. Strong $B$: Zeeman dominates, $|m_l,m_s\rangle$ with $\Delta E=\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)$ plus spin-orbit as a small correction.</details>

blocks.html:
• What exactly did EPR find paradoxical?
  • What do “local hidden variables” assume, and why does it give a bound of 2?

Script (German) 10.1–10.2, pp. 108–110. Look for: the EPR pair (10.1), local hidden-variable expectation values (10.2)-(10.3), the CHSH form (10.4)-(10.8), the quantum correlation $C(\vec n_1,\vec n_2)=-\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2$ (10.11) and the violation.

Prove (10.5) in two lines.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>If $A=A^\prime$: $A+A^\prime=\pm2$, $A-A^\prime=0$; if $A=-A^\prime$: the reverse. So $(A+A^\prime)B+(A-A^\prime)B^\prime=\pm2$, and averaging gives $|\dots|\le2$.</details>

Find angles where the singlet violates CHSH.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>With $C=-\cos\theta$: $\vec n_1,\vec n_1^\prime$ at $0^\circ,90^\circ$, $\vec n_2,\vec n_2^\prime$ at $45^\circ,-45^\circ$ give $|C+C+C-C|=4\cos45^\circ=2\sqrt2>2$.</details>

check.q: For the singlet, $C(\vec n_1,\vec n_2)=\langle\sigma^{(1)}_{\vec n_1}\sigma^{(2)}_{\vec n_2}\rangle=$
The maximal quantum value of the CHSH combination is

blocks.html:
• How can a continuous state be transmitted with two bits?
  • Why does this not allow signalling faster than light?

Script (German) 10.3, pp. 111–113. Look for: the three-particle state (10.14), the Bell-basis projectors $P_i=|\chi_i\rangle\langle\chi_i|$ (10.15), the four post-measurement states and the table of Bob’s operations.

Without Alice’s bits, what state does Bob have?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Each outcome has probability $\frac14$ and leaves a unitary image of $|\varphi\rangle$; averaged, Bob holds $\frac12\mathbb 1$: no information.</details>

Verify one row of the table: outcome 3 and $\sigma_1$.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Bob holds $|\downarrow\rangle\langle\uparrow|\varphi\rangle+|\uparrow\rangle\langle\downarrow|\varphi\rangle$; $\sigma_1$ swaps $\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$ and gives $|\varphi\rangle$.</details>

options: an entangled pair and 2 classical bits

blocks.html:
• What do you expand, and which convention fixes the expansion?
  • When is perturbation theory reliable?

Script (German) 11.1, pp. 114–117. Look for: $H=H_0+\lambda H^\prime$, power series in $\lambda$ for $\psi$ and $E$, projecting the order-$\lambda^s$ equation on $\psi_n$, $E^{(1)}$, $E^{(2)}$, $\psi^{(1)}$, the perturbed oscillator (11.1.1).

Derive $E^{(1)}$ and $E^{(2)}$.<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Order 1: $(H_0-E_n)\psi^{(1)}=(E^{(1)}-H^\prime)\psi_n$; project on $\psi_n$: $E^{(1)}=\langle n|H^\prime|n\rangle$, and $\psi^{(1)}=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{\langle m|H^\prime|n\rangle}{E_n-E_m}\psi_m$. Order 2 projected: $E^{(2)}=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{|\langle m|H^\prime|n\rangle|^2}{E_n-E_m}$.</details>
Why is $E^{(2)}$ of the ground state never positive?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>All $E_0-E_m<0$ and the numerators are non-negative: levels repel, the lowest is pushed down.</details>

enc.title: Read 11.2: degenerate perturbation theory and the Stark effect

blocks.html:
• Why does the non-degenerate formula break down for degenerate levels?
  • How can a symmetry save you the diagonalisation?
Script (German) 11.2, pp. 118–123. Look for: diagonalising $H^\prime$ in the degenerate subspace (11.2.1-11.2.2), lifting at second order (11.2.3), the linear Stark effect of $n=2$ (11.2.4).

Stark effect for $n=2$: why do only $|200\rangle$ and $|210\rangle$ mix?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$H^\prime=-eEz$ is odd under parity and commutes with $L_z$: it connects $l=0\leftrightarrow1$ with the same $m$. Only $\langle200|z|210\rangle\ne0$ (magnitude $3a$).</details>

Result for $n=2$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Two levels shift by $\pm3eEa$ (states $(|200\rangle\mp|210\rangle)/\sqrt2$), $|21\pm1\rangle$ stay: a linear Stark effect, possible because of the $l$-degeneracy.</details>

enc.title: Read 11.3: time-dependent perturbation theory and the golden rule

blocks.html:
• How do you organise the time evolution when $H$ depends on time?
  • Why does a transition probability turn into a constant rate?

Script (German) 11.3, pp. 124–132. Look for: the propagator $U(t,t_0)$ and its time-ordered exponential (11.3.1), the Heisenberg picture (11.3.2), the Dirac picture (11.88)-(11.95), first-order amplitude (11.98), sudden switch-on (11.100), Fermi’s golden rule (11.106) and its time window (Abb. 23).

Why is time ordering needed in $U(t,t_0)$?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>$H(t)$ at different times need not commute; the Dyson series orders later times to the left. If $H$ commutes with itself at all times, $U=e^{-\frac i\hbar\int H}$.</details>

For $H^\prime=V\theta(t)$, how does $P_{i\to f}$ behave at $\omega_{if}=0$ and how wide is the peak?<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Height $|V_{fi}|^2t^2/\hbar^2$, zeros at $\omega_{if}t=2n\pi$, width $\sim2\pi/t$: area $\propto t$, hence a rate $\Gamma=\frac{2\pi}\hbar|V_{fi}|^2\rho(E_f)$.</details>
